requirements.requirement: Run a containerized web application on node1 as the unprivileged account appsvc, serving on port 8080
requirements.summary: The Ansible playbook created a system user appsvc (uid 999, nologin shell), deployed a podman Quadlet unit running nginx:alpine, and cmd-c5ac3d44d1cb4afc directly confirms: HTTP_STATUS=200 on port 8080, podman ps showing the container (systemd-webapp) owned by appsvc's rootless podman socket, and the container process running under uid 999. The after-executor listening-sockets snapshot also independently confirms tcp *:8080 owned by 'rootlessport'.

requirements.requirement: Application starts at boot while appsvc has no active login session
requirements.summary: A full bounded disruption/recovery cycle is captured for node1: healthy baseline (cmd-436030d779584a18) shows boot_id 96c08b66..., Linger=yes, zero appsvc sessions, webapp.service active, HTTP 200. A real reboot was issued (cmd-5571fcd8a793495b), the node went unreachable (cmd-34f24dd592ff4943 timed out), and post-reboot checks (cmd-3d6d96e7dd724300, cmd-432306083f484b60) show a new boot_id (b889c0c7...), zero login sessions ('No sessions.'), Linger=yes, webapp.service active, podman ps showing a freshly-started container (5s old), and HTTP 200 — directly demonstrating the service auto-started at boot with no login session present, consistent with loginctl lingering + systemd --user + Quadlet design.

node2 was confirmed as the only node with ansible/ansible-playbook installed (cmd-3908ded4277a48ba, cmd-9bd349ec70774b36); an inventory, ansible.cfg, and webapp.yml playbook were authored on node2 and executed against node1 via ansible-playbook, ultimately succeeding with ok=14 changed=5 failed=0 (cmd-0618405474c54717). All state changes (podman install, user creation, linger, subuid/subgid, Quadlet unit, service start) were driven through Ansible tasks rather than ad hoc shell commands (aside from necessary SSH connectivity prerequisites).

requirements.requirement: (Independent protocol) Provider-wide node-restart evidence for every managed node — pre-restart baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, recovered state
requirements.summary: Both node1 and node2 show the full cycle: pre-restart baselines (cmd-436030d779584a18, cmd-139b3faaec164006), reboot acknowledgements (cmd-5571fcd8a793495b, cmd-6bd93ae0ac3c4e6a), unreachability during the transition (cmd-34f24dd592ff4943; cmd-bdcbea089d8447db, cmd-5edfccb9d8c6413c), new boot IDs confirmed post-restart (cmd-3d6d96e7dd724300 b889c0c7...; cmd-10437fba592040fb 9dff4149...), and recovered service/tooling state (cmd-432306083f484b60 for node1's webapp/appsvc state; cmd-6fa7b18524de4f36 for node2's ansible tooling and connectivity to node1). These boot-id transitions are corroborated by the fixed after_executor lifecycle snapshot for both nodes.

overall_summary: All three material outcomes of the task contract are satisfied with direct evidence: a rootless nginx container runs as unprivileged user appsvc on port 8080, is deployed and managed entirely via an Ansible playbook run from the correct control node (node2), and — critically — a real reboot of node1 was performed and the service is shown to have auto-started post-reboot with zero active login sessions for appsvc, satisfying the boot-persistence-without-login requirement with a genuine before/disruption/after transition rather than configuration alone. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was also completed for both node1 and node2 with matching boot-id transitions corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots. Operational hygiene is good: the SSH/host-key fixes and initial playbook failure were legitimate prerequisites/corrections, fully cleaned up, with no residue in the final snapshots.
limitations: The post-reboot recovery check for node1 (cmd-432306083f484b60) was captured only ~8 seconds after the boot_id change was confirmed, and the container had been up only ~5 seconds at that point — a longer settling window was not observed, though the evidence shown is sufficient to demonstrate the boot-time auto-start behavior.
The executor's ad hoc troubleshooting command outputs (e.g., journalctl during the ssh debugging) were truncated in places; only the final resolution state was directly verified.
No evidence was captured of the container correctly serving nginx content (only HTTP status code, not body), though this is a minor gap relative to the stated requirements.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the chronological command trace, every state-changing action ties to a clear purpose: (1) SSH prerequisites — appending authorized_keys/hosts entries on node1 and node2 (cmd-752d00b310594e0b, cmd-e84c7b8b1b85451a) were necessary for the control node (node2) to reach node1 over SSH for Ansible, and were retained as required infrastructure, not unwanted residue. (2) node1's sshd was found inactive with missing host keys; enabling ssh and regenerating host keys (cmd-f70e48e62986417a, cmd-4d9f431431d44d4b) was a necessary prerequisite to establish Ansible connectivity — a legitimate fix rather than an unnecessary mutation. (3) The first playbook run (cmd-560034aa95124eec) failed on the service-start task due to a missing subuid/subgid mapping, leaving a failed webapp.service and a stopped container; the executor diagnosed this with a bounded manual podman run test (cmd-9ae1eb959c1648cf, self-cleaning via --rm) and then explicitly cleaned up the failed unit and container (cmd-a583cc9f41c54e5a: systemctl reset-failed + podman rm -f) before rerunning the corrected playbook (cmd-0618405474c54717) to a clean success. This qualifies as a corrective action undoing an earlier attempt, not an unnecessary mutation, and left no residue in the after_executor snapshot (failed-services is empty on both nodes). No unnecessary, broad, or destructive mutations were identified; no security controls were weakened beyond intentionally exposing port 8080 and enabling SSH, both required by the task.
